**Steps of construction**

**(a)** Draw BC = 5 cm. With B and C as centres and radius 5 cm, draw arcs cutting each other at A. Join AB and AC. ABC is the equilateral triangle of side 5 cm.

**(b)** Draw the perpendicular bisectors of AB and BC. Let them meet at O. With O as centre and OA as radius, draw a circle; it passes through A, B and C. This is the circumcircle (radius \(= \frac{5}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 2.9\) cm on measuring).

**(c)** The locus of points equidistant from AB and BC is the bisector of \(\angle ABC\). With B as centre draw an arc cutting BA and BC; from these two points draw equal arcs meeting at a point, and join B to it, producing the line to meet the circumcircle again. Mark this point D. (In an equilateral triangle this bisector passes through the circumcentre O, so BD is a diameter.)

**(d)** Join AD and DC. Since D is on the bisector of \(\angle ABC\), arc AD = arc DC, so DA = DC. Also BA = BC = 5 cm. A quadrilateral with two pairs of equal adjacent sides is a **kite**. So ABCD is a kite (a cyclic kite, with \(\angle BAD = \angle BCD = 90^\circ\) because BD is a diameter, and \(\angle ADC = 120^\circ\)).

LHS \(= (\sec\theta - \cos\theta)(\operatorname{cosec}\theta - \sin\theta)\)

\(= \left(\frac{1}{\cos\theta} - \cos\theta\right)\left(\frac{1}{\sin\theta} - \sin\theta\right)\)

\(= \frac{1 - \cos^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \times \frac{1 - \sin^2\theta}{\sin\theta}\)

\(= \frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos\theta} \times \frac{\cos^2\theta}{\sin\theta}\) (using \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\))

\(= \sin\theta\cos\theta =\) RHS.

Hence proved.
